Computed tomography of the chest Extrinsic compression of the heart, in this patient by the sternum and anterior chest wall, can mimic some echocardiographic features of CP by enhancing ventricular interaction. The key to the correct diagnosis requires an awareness of (1) symptomatic PEX and (2) overinterpretation of TTE Doppler findings. PEX is the most common chest wall abnormality, occurring in 1 in 300 births,1and is characterized by posterior displacement of the chest wall, which alters standard echocardiographic views. There are several characteristic echocardiographic findings that should raise suspicion for severe PEX. First, extrinsic compression of the anterior cardiac chambers, especially the right ventricle (RV), alters the orientation of the heart and often requires the use of nonstandard imaging windows.2Second, extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers is often positional (worse with sitting, leaning forward) and exacerbated during expiration, which may result in altered venous return, RV obstruction, and reduced RV stroke volume.2Extrinsic compression of the right-sided chambers can also produce ventricular interdependence, respirophasic septal motion, and abnormal venous return that may mimic constrictive physiology.2-5Additionally, pericardial effusions are common in both PEX and CP.2-5Recognition of chest wall deformities and integration with clinical and imaging context are critical to avoid misdiagnosis. In this patient, there is a prominent ventricular septal bounce (Figure 1A) but absence of respirophasic septal shift. Elevated medial e′ mitral annulus velocity (≥0.09 m/s) is a common diagnostic feature of CP4; however, higher velocities are normal in younger individuals, like this patient, and the absence of annulus reversus further argues against CP. Mild enlargement of the inferior vena cava is frequently seen in younger individuals, and normal inspiratory collapse is uncommon with CP.4Although prominent expiratory diastolic reversals in the HV Doppler are a specific finding for CP, this patient had persistence of hepatic diastolic flow reversals throughout the respiratory cycle (Figure 1D), which, together with the absence of transmitral forward flow, reflects altered compliance of the RV due to extrinsic compression by the sternum and chest wall (Figure 1E).2Increased respirophasic variation in tricuspid inflow Doppler velocity (not shown) was initially reported in a small series of 7 patients with CP3; however, subsequent studies have demonstrated this finding lacks sensitivity for CP,5and the specificity for differentiating CP from extrinsic compression of the heart is uncertain. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) enables simultaneous visualization of thoracic and cardiac anatomy without limitation by acoustic windows, enabling differentiation of PEX from CP. Chest computed tomography (CT) is also useful for confirming PEX by quantifying disease severity using the Haller index, the ratio of the transverse diameter to the anteroposterior diameter of the chest.1,2These imaging modalities complement echocardiography when findings are ambiguous. PEX can produce echocardiographic findings that mimic CP, including ventricular septal bounce, increased tricuspid inflow variation, and abnormal superior vena cava and HV Doppler flow. Standard TTE views can be obscured in PEX, whereas MRI and CT imaging views are typically unaffected. Integration of imaging findings with clinical context is essential to distinguish extrinsic cardiac compression from true CP. The patient underwent chest CT (Figure 2), which confirmed severe PEX (Haller index 3.78), as well as cardiac MRI, which demonstrated RV free wall compression by PEX without constrictive physiology. Treatment options were discussed, including Nuss repair, but the patient elected not to pursue surgical correction at this time. He was counseled on exercise training along with physical therapy for postural and chest expansion exercises.

In this case, there was an activation time delay between the LV segments adjacent to the papillary muscles, resulting in inadequate tethering forces on the mitral valve and failure of coaptation.1 Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) with biventricular pacing (BVP) represents the criterion standard of care for patients with severe secondary MR and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) with a QRS duration greater than 130 ms with LBBB, as outlined in the 2021 European Society of Cardiology guidelines.2,3Mitral valve surgery is recommended if symptoms persist after optimization of conventional heart failure therapy, including CRT (class 1 recommendation), while transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) might be considered in some patients (class 2A). In the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology guidelines, TEER (class 2A) is preferred over surgical repair or replacement (class 2B).4 Regarding the treatment of MR, CRT facilitates the coordination of tethering forces on the papillary muscles, thereby enhancing the surface area for leaflet coaptation,1with an immediate reduction in MR. An additional remote effect is reverse remodeling of the LV, which may take from weeks to months. Left bundle branch pacing (LBBP) is emerging as a potential alternative to BVP in CRT. Two international case-control studies5,6suggested superior electromechanical resynchronization and higher rates of clinical and echocardiographic response with LBBP in HFrEF in comparison with BVP. Conversely, severe MR with permanent LBBB and LV or left atrial dilation may not elicit an immediate response, as it would be mediated by reverse remodeling instead. case_meta.explanation: Preexcitation syndrome with de Winter ECG pattern D. Emergent coronary angiography according to STEMI Initial ECG (Figure 1) showed type A preexcitation syndrome, with obvious ST-segment depression in leads V3through V5and positive delta wave (poor skin-electrode contact in lead V2) that could not be explained by secondary ST-segment change. The findings seemed consistent with non-STEMI acute coronary syndrome (C). However, the ST-segment depression was in an upward concave pattern (not downsloping), followed by tall and positive T waves (not inverted), which are not consistent with non-STEMI. The aforementioned characteristic features are consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes in preexcitation syndrome and primary ST-T changes in de Winter ECG pattern, which is widely recognized as signifying acute proximal left anterior descending (LAD) coronary artery occlusion.1These ECG changes warranted consideration of emergent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) as STEMI equivalent (D). Coronary angiography revealed 100% obstruction of the proximal to mid LAD coronary artery. After PCI with stent implantation, the patient’s symptoms disappeared, with a thrombolysis in MI flow grade of 3. The postprocedure ECG (Figure 2) showed that the QRS morphology was identical to that recorded during the initial ECG but with disappearance of the depressed ST-segment and tall T waves, suggesting that an acute STEMI had not occurred. Paradoxically, preexcitation was not present in the sixth beat, which showed abnormal Q waves in leads V1through V3and ST-segment elevation in leads V1through V5. These ECG changes indicated an acute, extensive anterior wall STEMI. The de Winter ECG pattern, which is highly predictive for acute occlusion of the proximal LAD, has been observed in 2% of cases with LAD occlusions.1,2This ECG pattern is characterized by upsloping ST-segment depression with tall and symmetrically peaked T waves in leads V1through V4(or V6). The clinical implications are equivalent to new ST-segment elevation with symptoms of myocardial ischemia.1-4It implies the need for urgent coronary angiography with the possibility of PCI to avoid progression to acute MI. However, STEMI may also occur before PCI, as in the present case. Interesting findings include, first, that the diagnosis of de Winter ECG pattern was not impeded by the presence of preexcitation syndrome in the initial ECG, which can provide important diagnostic clues. Second, without symptoms, the postprocedure ECG seemed that the patient did not have an acute MI, which was actually masked by preexcitation syndrome (but unmasked in a single, non-preexcited beat). In patients with preexcitation syndrome, the positive delta wave may mask the necrotic Q wave and secondary ST-T wave may influence ischemia-induced ST-T change.5,6However, this case emphasizes that the presence of preexcitation syndrome may not conceal the changes of the de Winter ECG pattern. The ECG features in patients with type A preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern may be consistent with the effects of combined secondary ST-T changes and primary ST-T changes. Namely, ST-segment depression is in an upward concave pattern followed by tall and positive T waves in leads V1through V4(and V6). Both preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern have ST-segment depression that is in a downsloping pattern with flat or inverted T waves in the former and an upsloping pattern with tall and positive T waves in the latter. Persisting chest pain can provide additional important information for diagnosis. To our knowledge, this is the first described case of intermittent loss of preexcitation in preexcitation syndrome and de Winter ECG pattern. These ECG changes indicated the presence of an acute extensive anterior wall STEMI, providing evidence for need of further treatment. The repeat troponin I level was 4.57 ng/mL (reference, <0.028 ng/mL) 8 hours after the procedure. Repeat ECG 34 hours after PCI showed intermittent loss of preexcitation, and the ST-segment elevation and abnormal Q waves were identical to that recorded in the sixth beat in the postprocedure ECG, verifying that an acute STEMI had occurred. Routine postprocedural therapy was performed after PCI. The patient was discharged home with routine management following PCI in the setting of STEMI, and he also was referred to a cardiac rehabilitation program.

Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate Flecainide is a class Ic antiarrhythmic drug. It delays phase 0 depolarization of the action potential by blocking cardiac voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.5, resulting in slowing of conduction.1,2Its major use is in the treatment and prevention of symptomatic AF and supraventricular tachycardias. Contraindications include bundle branch block, cardiomyopathies, and significant liver or kidney impairment. The usual dose of flecainide is 50 to 150 mg every 12 hours. The half-life is 12 to 27 hours. It undergoes hepatic oxidation by cytochrome P450 (CYP2D6 isoform); however, approximately 80% of clearance is by the kidneys; thus, dosing must be reduced to 50 mg twice daily if there is kidney failure.3Notably, hemodialysis is not an effective method for clearance due to the large volume of distribution.4Aside from kidney and liver failure, toxic effects can occur with hypovolemia, hypokalemia, and hyponatremia and in patients who carry alleles that decrease their ability to metabolize CYP2D. Acute toxic effects can present with dizziness, seizures, visual disturbance, sinus arrest, atrioventricular (AV) block, and ventricular tachyarrhythmias.5Toxic effects should be suspected if the QRS duration increases by 50% or if the PR interval increases by 30%.6Prominent terminal R waves (≥3 mm) in lead aVR are a sensitive predictor of toxic effects (Figure 1).7Treatment of hemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmias should include cardioversion. Amiodarone may be used to suppress ventricular tachycardia (VT). Bradyarrhythmias may require transvenous pacing. Closer inspection of this patient’s ECG on admission at our hospital (Figure 2) showed that the rhythm was atrial flutter (AFL) with an atrial cycle length of 230 milliseconds and 2:1 AV conduction.
